8DZsq_qAVI4.title: The Philosophy of Islamic Thought #3: The Theory of Knowledge in Islam
8DZsq_qAVI4.one_line: Islamic epistemology: revelation, reason and the senses, how they are tested and reconciled, and how the theological schools ranked them.
8DZsq_qAVI4.summary: He argues that Islam's theory of knowledge was mature far earlier than most systems and lays out its parts. Knowledge comes from revelation, reason and the senses, including intuition, which he says drives most scientific and medical breakthroughs. A conclusion is sound when it is authentically transmitted, congruent with reason and corresponds to reality. Faith rests on self-evident universal truths: reason deduces a Creator from constants like day and night, not from shifting variables, and infinite regress is irrational. Yet reason cannot provide guidance, know Allah's attributes or comprehend divinity, so knowing its limits matters. When text and reason seem to clash, both the interpretation and the logic must be revised, with experience helping. He distinguishes obedience-based from purpose-based rulings, illustrated by the Maliki and majority positions on a dog's saliva, and explains the logic of inheritance shares. He surveys the Mu'tazili, Ash'ari, Maturidi and Athari positions, insisting none rejected reason; the debate was how reason serves revelation. Finally he grades evidence by sanctity, authenticity and indication, warning people not to fire a single hadith at others, since the imams weighed all evidence. He concludes that Islamic epistemology is realist, theistic and integrative, grounded in epistemic humility.

outline.heading: Islam as an ideology, not a reduced religion
outline.gist: Boxing Islam into the masjid, the heart or the state shrinks it; din means a complete way of seeing and living.

outline.heading: Why epistemology comes first
outline.gist: Every ideology must explain how it knows what it knows; Islam's theory of knowledge impressed even non-Muslims.

outline.heading: Andalusian libraries and the European scientific rise
outline.gist: Muslims translated and credited knowledge from every civilization; he believes the books left in Andalusia fast-tracked modern science.

outline.heading: Three sources of knowledge and how they differ
outline.gist: All Muslim schools accept revelation, reason and the senses; other ideologies drop one, and the senses include experience that reason cannot yet explain.

outline.heading: Three tests of a true conclusion
outline.gist: Authentic transmission, cognitive congruence with reason, and correspondence to reality shown through real examples.

outline.heading: Intuition drives discovery
outline.gist: Most scientific and medical breakthroughs begin as a hunch later proven; discarding the senses is immature.

outline.heading: Applying the tests to every Islamic claim
outline.gist: From washing in wudu to the existence of Allah, all three must line up; this raises the question of reason's uses and limits.

outline.heading: Self-evident universal truths
outline.gist: Gravity, day and night, time and other minds need no proof; scholars wary of science are really saying a theory is not yet a self-evident truth to build faith on.

outline.heading: Intellect is the basis of religious accountability
outline.gist: Revelation is understood only through reason; those without it, like a demented elderly father, carry no obligation.

outline.heading: Intellect cannot provide guidance: Adam and the names
outline.gist: Raw reason deduces much but cannot give direction; Allah answered the angels by teaching Adam names, showing the human power to reason.

outline.heading: Allah is known from constants, not variables
outline.gist: Iman is deduced from self-evident truths; the Quran points to simple constants like birth, the sun and the rivers rather than complex details.

outline.heading: Learning from every clue except the biggest ones
outline.gist: Like detectives or children reading a room, we deduce from small clues, yet scientism deduces nothing from the existence of the universe itself.

outline.heading: A Creator as a self-evident truth by proxy
outline.gist: Every constant points to one unity behind creation; infinite regress is anti-rational because time would never reach today.

outline.heading: Attributes need revelation; divinity exceeds the mind
outline.gist: We cannot picture a being without beginning, end or space; a comprehensible god would just be a mighty creature like Greek myths.

outline.heading: Reason is powerful but not absolute
outline.gist: The mind sails freely until it hits a membrane of time and space; ignoring that limit leaves people going in circles.

outline.heading: Cognitive dissonance and youth leaving the faith
outline.gist: A survey found religious people's conduct the top push factor, but for youth the clash between what they are taught and what they experience is decisive.

outline.heading: When text and reason clash, revise both
outline.gist: The Quran is never wrong, but an interpretation or a chain of logic may be; experience and social norms help realign them without acting as judge.

outline.heading: Obedience-based versus purpose-based rulings
outline.gist: Some rulings carry a clear legal reason, others are pure worship whose reason we do not know.

outline.heading: Legal reason versus wisdom: the pork example
outline.gist: Health benefits are wisdom, not the operative reason, so engineering a healthy pig does not lift the prohibition.

outline.heading: Case study: a dog's saliva, the majority and Imam Malik
outline.gist: Both narrate the seven-washings hadith; Malik argues living creatures are pure by nature and reads the washing differently.

outline.heading: Is the seven-fold washing purification or worship?
outline.gist: If it is worship, the vessel is still pure and usable; the whole difference turns on classifying the ruling's type.

outline.heading: Inheritance shares and the duty of financial care
outline.gist: Men inherit more because they must support the women around them; the mistake lies in abandoning that norm, not in the verse.

outline.heading: Necessary and acquired knowledge; certainty and probability
outline.gist: Deniers of self-evident truth are not worth debating; law and life, like marriage decisions, run on high probability.

outline.heading: The Mu'tazila: primacy of reason
outline.gist: They held reason discovers morality independently and reinterpreted conflicting texts metaphorically; an island-raised child shows why this cannot be tested.

outline.heading: The Ash'aris: reason establishes revelation, revelation guides reason
outline.gist: Human readiness to enslave one another shows morality needs revelation; reason first proves the message, then follows it.

outline.heading: The Maturidis: middle rationalism
outline.gist: Reason knows God and basic morals, while revelation supplies detailed law and the unseen.

outline.heading: The Atharis: primacy of revelation
outline.gist: Literal acceptance and suspicion of Greek philosophy, yet Ibn Taymiyyah argued sound reason and authentic revelation always agree.

outline.heading: No school rejected reason
outline.gist: The real debate was never reason versus revelation but how far reason serves revelation.

outline.heading: Grading evidence: sanctity, authenticity, indication
outline.gist: Texts can be definitive or probable in authenticity and meaning, as with the word qur' in the waiting period, producing layered grades of evidence.

outline.heading: Do not shoot people with a single hadith
outline.gist: A hadith is one piece of evidence; following an imam respects how the imams weighed all of it together.

outline.heading: Individual ruling, law and constitution
outline.gist: Learning lets you practise yourself; issuing rulings for others requires judge-level mastery.

outline.heading: Each imam's algorithm for weighing evidence
outline.gist: Abu Hanifa's caution with certain narrators' legal reports is method, not disrespect; studying it makes you love the din.

outline.heading: Disputed sources and the practice of Madinah
outline.gist: Where no specific text exists, Malik trusted the practice he saw among the people of Madinah.

outline.heading: Conclusion: a realist, theistic, integrative model
outline.gist: The universe is knowable because of divine unity; knowledge integrates all three sources with epistemic humility.

outline.heading: Outro

48:29.ar: مُّحَمَّدࣱ رَّسُولُ ٱللَّهِۚ وَٱلَّذِينَ مَعَهُۥٓ أَشِدَّآءُ عَلَى ٱلۡكُفَّارِ رُحَمَآءُ بَيۡنَهُمۡۖ تَرَىٰهُمۡ رُكَّعࣰ ا سُجَّدࣰ ا يَبۡتَغُونَ فَضۡلࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرِضۡوَٰنࣰ اۖ سِيمَاهُمۡ فِي وُجُوهِهِم مِّنۡ أَثَرِ ٱلسُّجُودِۚ ذَٰلِكَ مَثَلُهُمۡ فِي ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةِۚ وَمَثَلُهُمۡ فِي ٱلۡإِنجِيلِ كَزَرۡعٍ أَخۡرَجَ شَطۡـَٔهُۥ فَـَٔازَرَهُۥ فَٱسۡتَغۡلَظَ فَٱسۡتَوَىٰ عَلَىٰ سُوقِهِۦ يُعۡجِبُ ٱلزُّرَّاعَ لِيَغِيظَ بِهِمُ ٱلۡكُفَّارَۗ وَعَدَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ مِنۡهُم مَّغۡفِرَةࣰ وَأَجۡرًا عَظِيمَۢا
48:29.en: Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; and those with him are forceful against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating [in prayer], seeking bounty from Allah and [His] pleasure. Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration. That is their description in the Torah. And their description in the Gospel is as a plant which produces its offshoots and strengthens them so they grow firm and stand upon their stalks, delighting the sowers - so that Allah may enrage by them the disbelievers. Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds among them forgiveness and a great reward

49:12.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱجۡتَنِبُواْ كَثِيرࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلظَّنِّ إِنَّ بَعۡضَ ٱلظَّنِّ إِثۡمࣱۖ وَلَا تَجَسَّسُواْ وَلَا يَغۡتَب بَّعۡضُكُم بَعۡضًاۚ أَيُحِبُّ أَحَدُكُمۡ أَن يَأۡكُلَ لَحۡمَ أَخِيهِ مَيۡتࣰ ا فَكَرِهۡتُمُوهُۚ وَٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ تَوَّابࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
49:12.en: O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy or backbite each other. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when dead? You would detest it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful

51:22.en: And in the heaven is your provision and whatever you are promised

51:23.ar: فَوَرَبِّ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ إِنَّهُۥ لَحَقࣱّ مِّثۡلَ مَآ أَنَّكُمۡ تَنطِقُونَ
51:23.en: Then by the Lord of the heaven and earth, indeed, it is truth - just as [sure as] it is that you are speaking

GQDGbOZN3c0.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 25 - Quranic Themes: Similes and Examples
GQDGbOZN3c0.one_line: Why the Quran teaches through similes, worked through the crop simile of 48:29, the corpse simile for backbiting in 49:12, and provision in 51:22-23.
GQDGbOZN3c0.summary: He treats the Quran's similes and examples as a theme of their own, separate from its stories. Human learning depends on examples: a concept stays uncertain until an example lands, and a poor or partial example makes people doubt the point itself, so he refuses to teach anything he cannot illustrate. The Quran's examples have stayed accurate and relevant across centuries, which is part of why its guidance kept its credibility, while a preacher's examples date within a generation. He then works through three passages. In 48:29 the companions are described twice: in the Torah by five plain traits, and in the Gospel as a crop that sprouts weakly, is supported, thickens and stands. He reads the second as the pattern for dawah and for raising the next generation: patient, gentle, daily care that never stops, which is why Muslim communities in the West must put education and mentorship first and let their youth practise in the masjid. In 49:12 he explains why eating a dead brother's flesh fits backbiting on three counts: the absent cannot defend themselves, something is taken from them, and the gain is a disgusting boost to one's own ego. Finally 51:22-23 swears that provision is as certain as people's talking, so worry and haram earnings are pointless.

outline.heading: Opening
Similes as a Quranic theme, distinct from stories
outline.gist: The Quran constantly says 'this is like that'; people need an example before a concept feels rational, and they test the example against the concept.

outline.heading: No example, no teaching
outline.gist: A bad or partial example makes listeners question the point; he will not teach a concept until he finds an example that fully fits, or people will misapply it.

outline.heading: The Quran as master of examples
outline.gist: Had its examples been weak, the Quran would have lost its ethical and legal credibility over time; their accuracy is what kept it.

outline.heading: Examples that do not expire
outline.gist: Irrelevant examples lose an audience and a 1985 lecture's examples already feel foreign, yet the Quran's stay applicable in every era; scholars have written whole books on its similes.

outline.heading: 48:29 and the three surahs about the Prophet
outline.gist: Muhammad, al-Fath and al-Hujurat form a cluster teaching who the Prophet is and how to follow him; al-Fath closes with a verse full of similes.

outline.heading: Firm with enemies, merciful with each other
outline.gist: Strictness is for those who attack your rights, never for fellow Muslims; the companions are constantly bowing, prostrating and seeking Allah's bounty and pleasure.

outline.heading: Their description in the Torah: five traits
outline.gist: The Torah's description is plain and practical: strength against enemies, compassion, ongoing prayer, connection with Allah and seeking only His favour; he notes how translations obscured these prophecies.

outline.heading: The mark of prostration is serenity in the face
outline.gist: Not the callus on the forehead but inner calm that shows on the face; people read faces instinctively, and long prostration leaves its blessing there.

outline.heading: Their description in the Gospel: the growing crop
outline.gist: A shoot breaks from the seed, is propped up, thickens and stands on its stalk, delighting the sowers and vexing rivals; he explains kuffar here as farmers who cover seed with soil.

outline.heading: Dawah as planting seeds one by one
outline.gist: His favourite of the two similes: Muslims plant seeds of iman in people and in the next generation, as the Prophet taught and protected each companion individually.

outline.heading: Gentle, patient care that never ends
outline.gist: The weak shoot needs protecting, then encouragement even once strong; nobody yells at a seed or uproots it for growing slowly, and a tree takes a decade of daily attention.

outline.heading: His uncle talking to the apricot trees
outline.gist: In Syria he once found his elderly uncle greeting and stroking his trees; that tenderness is the picture of how Muslims are meant to nurture.

outline.heading: What Muslim communities in the West are for
outline.gist: Any vision for Muslim communities that does not centre education and mentorship of the next generation, building their identity, voice and courage, misses the point of this simile.

outline.heading: The masjid as the training ground for youth
outline.gist: Let nervous young people lead prayer and make mistakes; every child in the masjid is ours, and if we do not nurture them someone else will make them their crop.

outline.heading: 49:12: avoid most assumptions
outline.gist: Al-Hujurat is the surah of etiquette; the mind fills gaps with suspicion, and the rule is to avoid most of something when some of it is harmful.

outline.heading: No spying, no backbiting, and the corpse simile
outline.gist: Do not chase people's secrets or speak behind their backs; would you eat your dead brother's flesh? You would hate it, so hate backbiting.

outline.heading: Interlude
Three ways the simile fits
outline.gist: The absent cannot defend themselves, you take their dignity and reputation, and your gain is a rotten boost to your ego from putting them down.

outline.heading: Legitimate talk versus the taste of backbiting
outline.gist: Parents, caregivers and mentors may discuss someone in their care; backbiting is the talk with no protective purpose that you crave and savour.

outline.heading: 51:22-23: provision is as certain as your talking
outline.gist: Allah swears that what is decreed for you is as real as the fact that people never stop talking, so there is no point in sleepless worry, broken relationships or haram earnings.

takeaways: Before teaching a point, find an example that fully fits it and fits the audience's life.
Treat dawah and youth work as patient seed planting: protect, support and keep encouraging people even once they are strong.
Let young people lead prayer and make mistakes in the masjid, and treat every child there as your own.
Avoid most assumptions, do not dig into people's private lives, and stop any talk about someone that serves no protective purpose.
Trust that provision is decreed and refuse worry or haram earnings as ways to secure it.
